title: Sell Mineral Rights in Washakie County, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Washakie County, WY | Bighorn Basin
metaDescription: Own oil, gas, or mineral rights in Washakie County, WY? We buy Bighorn Basin mineral interests around Worland and Ten Sleep. Free courthouse-checked offer.
heroLead: Washakie County has been producing oil out of the Bighorn Basin since before Wyoming had paved highways, and a lot of what's under the ground here is still held the way it was left by the original homestead patents.
intro: Washakie County sits in the middle of the Bighorn Basin, bounded by the Bighorn Mountains to the east and the Absarokas out west, with the Nowood River cutting through the southern part of the county on its way to join the Bighorn. Worland is the county seat, and the courthouse there holds the deed and probate records for just about every mineral interest tied to this ground going back to statehood-era homesteads.

This isn't a boomtown county. It's a working basin with a long production history, small towns, ranch families who've held the same section for four or five generations, and a courthouse staff that's used to pulling mineral deed books for people who moved away decades ago and still hold an interest their grandfather never sold.

sections.heading: The Geology Under Washakie County
paragraphs: The Bighorn Basin is layered oil country - the Tensleep Sandstone, named for the town just west of Worland, has been a workhorse producing zone across the basin for a hundred years. Below it sits the Phosphoria, and deeper still the Madison Limestone, both of which have paid off in various fields across the county over the decades. Shallower Cretaceous and Cloverly zones round out the picture on the flanks.

Washakie County's own production history runs through fields like Big Sand Draw and Winkleman Dome, structural traps that were found early in the basin's development and have been producing, declining, and getting re-worked in cycles ever since. It's mature basin behavior - steady decline curves, periodic re-entry and workover activity, not the sharp production spikes you'd see out of an unconventional shale play.

sections.heading: How Ownership Broke Up Here
paragraphs: Most of Washakie County's mineral ownership traces back to homestead patents from the early 1900s, when ranch families proved up 160 or 320 acre tracts along the Nowood and around the irrigated bottomland near Worland and Ten Sleep. Minerals often stayed with the surface at first, then got severed off in a lease or sale sometime in the 1930s through the 1950s as oil activity picked up in the basin.

What that means today is a lot of fractional ownership. A single quarter section might have eight or ten mineral owners on record, heirs of heirs, some still local, most scattered to Colorado, Montana, or further. Washakie County isn't checkerboard country the way southern Wyoming along the old Union Pacific grant is, but there's still meaningful federal minerals mixed with private ground here, tied to BLM administration rather than railroad grant history, which affects who you'd even lease with on a given tract.

Because the county's oil history is so long, it's also common to find mineral deeds with outdated legal descriptions, old unit designations that don't match how a tract is described today, or royalty interests that were carved out of a larger family estate and never cleanly re-recorded. None of that stops a sale, but it does mean the title work takes an actual look at the Washakie County Clerk's records rather than a rubber stamp.

sections.heading: Towns and Ground We Work Across the County
paragraphs: Worland anchors the county as both the seat and the population center, sitting on the Bighorn River with the courthouse, the clerk's office, and most of the county's services. Ten Sleep, up against the base of the Bighorn Mountains along the old stage route, gave its name to the Tensleep Sandstone and still has ranch families holding minerals from the original homestead era. Manderson and Hyattville round out the smaller communities, both closer to the basin's edge where production has historically been thinner but not absent.

We buy interests across all of it - producing royalty tied to a Tensleep well that's been paying small checks for decades, non-producing acreage that's never seen a rig, and fractional interests split among heirs who mostly just want the county tax notice and the annual division order paperwork to stop showing up.

sections.heading: What Selling Actually Involves
paragraphs: We start with the deed record at the Washakie County Clerk's office in Worland, confirm your net mineral acreage and legal description against what's actually recorded, and check current activity and historical production on the tract before we build a number. If there's an active royalty history, we look at the decline curve rather than just the last few checks, since a well three years into decline pays differently than one that's five years past its peak.

If you're an heir dealing with a fractional interest that's never been cleanly divided, we can usually work through that without forcing a full formal partition. Value talk here is always a range tied to production and basin activity - nobody selling minerals in a mature basin like this should be hearing a locked-in guaranteed number before the record's been checked.

faqs.question: Is Washakie County part of the Bighorn Basin checkerboard?
faqs.answer: No, the classic Wyoming checkerboard comes from the Union Pacific's railroad grant across southern counties like Sweetwater and Carbon. Washakie County has its own mix of private and federal minerals, tied more to BLM administration and original homestead patents than to railroad grant history.

faqs.question: What's the Tensleep Sandstone and why does it matter for my mineral rights?
faqs.answer: It's a major producing formation named for the town of Ten Sleep, and it's been the workhorse zone for Bighorn Basin oil production for a century. If your interest is in Washakie County, there's a good chance any historical production on it came from the Tensleep or the Phosphoria beneath it.

faqs.question: Where are mineral deeds and probate records kept for this county?
faqs.answer: At the Washakie County Clerk's office in Worland, the county seat. That's where we start every title check before making an offer.

faqs.question: I inherited a fractional mineral interest with several other heirs. Can you buy just my share?
faqs.answer: Yes. We regularly buy individual heir shares without requiring the whole family group to sell together or forcing a formal court partition.

faqs.question: Does an old well that stopped producing years ago still have value?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. A shut-in or plugged well can still leave the underlying mineral interest worth something if the tract has re-entry or offset potential, but we evaluate that on the specific well and formation rather than assuming.
